summary: Describes the problems of carrying IPv4 and IPv6 over IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) wireless broadband networks, pointing out gaps in the link layer's MAC design. It gives an overview of 802.16 network characteristics and convergence sublayers, and sets common terminology and goals for later solution documents. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: WiMAX is a wireless way to get internet, but its rules do not fit the internet's language perfectly. This paper lists the awkward spots so people can fix them.

questions: why is wimax hard for ip
subtitle: Finding the right way to run IP networks on wireless broadband.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 is a connection-oriented, point-to-point wireless technology that does not naturally fit how IP networks expect the link layer to work.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies what does not work when you try to run IPv4 and IPv6 over 802.16, describes the available link models (point-to-point and Ethernet-like), and lists the gaps that later RFCs need to solve.
tldr.outcome: The document provides a foundation for later protocol work by clearly naming the problems and setting common goals for the IETF.

facts.label: Convergence sublayer types
facts.value: ATM CS, Packet CS (IP, Ethernet, 802.1Q variants)

today: RFC 5154 is an Informational document that remains in effect. It serves as a foundational problem statement for IEEE 802.16 and IP integration work, with many follow-on RFCs addressing specific solutions to the gaps it identifies.

sections.title: IEEE 802.16 and the IP Problem
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16, also known as WiMAX and developed for broadband wireless access, is a connection-oriented, point-to-multipoint network. A central Base Station (BS) connects to multiple Subscriber Stations (SS), each through a dedicated point-to-point MAC connection. The IEEE 802.16 standard defines a convergence sublayer that bridges between the MAC layer and higher layers like IP and Ethernet.

The core problem is mismatch: IP networks normally expect the underlying link layer to behave like Ethernet (supporting broadcast and multicast to all nodes equally), or like a simple point-to-point link. IEEE 802.16 is point-to-point in its MAC design but arranged in a star topology, and it uses connection identifiers rather than MAC addresses. This creates practical problems when trying to configure IP subnets and run common protocols like address resolution and router discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: WiMAX is point-to-point (each device talks directly to the base station) but IP expects either everyone to be on the same network or one-to-one links. This mismatch breaks things.

sections.title: IEEE 802.16 MAC and Convergence Sublayers
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 uses transport connections: unidirectional MAC-level connections between a Subscriber Station and Base Station, each identified by a 16-bit Connection Identifier (CID). User data flows over these connections, not through MAC addresses. The PDU (Protocol Data Unit) sent over the air carries the CID but no source or destination address field.

The convergence sublayer sits above the MAC and is responsible for mapping between higher-layer data (like IP packets or Ethernet frames) and the MAC's connection-oriented service. It uses classifiers to decide which outbound packet should be sent over which connection. IEEE 802.16 defines two packet convergence sublayer types: the IP Convergence Sublayer (IP CS) for carrying IP packets directly, and the Ethernet Convergence Sublayer (Ethernet CS) for Ethernet-style frames. IPv4 and IPv6 have separate classifiers within IP CS.
sections.plainLanguage: WiMAX has labeled pipes (connections) instead of addresses. The convergence sublayer is a traffic cop that looks at each packet and sends it down the right pipe.

sections.title: Two Feasible IP Subnet Models
sections.content:
An IP Subnet is a topological area where all nodes share the same IP address prefix. IEEE 802.16's design allows two feasible approaches:

Point-to-Point Link Model (for IP CS): Each Subscriber Station resides on its own IP Subnet with the Access Router. This matches IP CS's direct IP packet carry and avoids the need for broadcast and multicast. However, it requires mechanisms to handle what would normally be done by ARP or Neighbor Discovery, and the Access Router must send unicast router advertisements and assign unique prefixes to each SS.

Ethernet-Like Link Model (for Ethernet CS): All Subscriber Stations under the same Access Router share the same IP Subnet, as if they were on an Ethernet. This works with Ethernet CS but requires additional features: IEEE 802.16 MAC is still connection-oriented and cannot natively broadcast or multicast, so bridging functionality must be added on top of the Base Station. Additionally, multicast and broadcast traffic can wake up Subscriber Stations in sleep or idle mode, which wastes battery power.
sections.plainLanguage: Either each wireless device gets its own private connection to the router (point-to-point), or they all share one network like Ethernet. Each choice has pros and cons.

sections.title: Key Problems in Each Model
sections.content:
Point-to-Point Model challenges: Address resolution protocols like ARP do not apply when IP CS is used, since the MAC layer has no addresses. Router advertisements must be sent unicast to each SS rather than broadcast. Each SS must be given a separate IP prefix. Neighbor Unreachability Detection and Duplicate Address Detection become simpler but still require clear specification.

Ethernet-Like Model challenges: Even though the CS presents an Ethernet interface, address resolution via broadcast ARP or Neighbor Discovery causes unnecessary multicast traffic. All Subscriber Stations are neighbors, so neighbor discovery affects many devices. Router advertisements to a multicast group wake up sleeping SSs. When an SS tries to talk to another SS on the same prefix, the Ethernet destination address is needed, but direct link-layer communication between SSs requires bridging functionality that IEEE 802.16 does not provide natively.

A third model, shared IPv6 prefix distribution, was identified as infeasible because it creates multi-link subnet problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Point-to-point is simple for addressing but needs custom handling. Ethernet-like needs broadcast and multicast, which breaks sleeping devices and requires extra work to emulate Ethernet.

sections.title: IETF Work Goals
sections.content:
The RFC identifies six goals for later IETF work to make IP over IEEE 802.16 practical:

First, define how to provide the point-to-point link model for IP CS, addressing the gaps in address resolution, router discovery, and prefix management. Second, reduce power consumption caused by multicast and broadcast waking sleep-mode devices in the Ethernet-like model. Third, avoid multi-link subnet problems. Fourth, allow applicability of security schemes like SEND (Secure Neighbor Discovery). Fifth, avoid introducing new security threats. Sixth, review and define management interfaces and models in collaboration with IEEE 802.16 working group.

This document is explicitly informational; it does not define solutions but rather lays out the landscape so other RFCs can tackle each problem systematically.
sections.plainLanguage: Later documents will need to solve these six problems: making point-to-point work, saving battery in shared mode, avoiding network confusion, keeping security strong, and managing the devices.
